title: Product of Array Except Self
directAnswer: answer[i] = product of everything left of i × product of everything right of i. Compute prefix products in one left-to-right pass, then multiply by suffix products in a right-to-left pass, reusing the output array so it's O(1) extra space. Division is banned (and breaks on zeros), so the two-pass prefix/suffix trick is the intended answer. O(n) time.

remember.formula:
res[i] = 1
prefix = 1
for i in range(n): res[i] = prefix; prefix *= nums[i]
suffix = 1
for i in range(n-1,-1,-1): res[i] *= suffix; suffix *= nums[i]
rules: `answer[i]` = (product of all left of i) × (product of all right of i) — never includes `nums[i]`.
**No division** — it's banned and undefined when any element is 0.
Write the **prefix** into `res` on the way right, then multiply by the running **suffix** on the way left.
Reuse the output array for prefixes so the running suffix scalar is the only extra state → `O(1)` extra space.
Seed both running products at **1** (multiplicative identity), and `res[0]`'s prefix is 1 (nothing to its left).
whenToUse: Each output depends on 'everything except me' aggregated multiplicatively or additively
Division is disallowed or unsafe (zeros, modular arithmetic)
You can precompute left/right partial aggregates in linear passes
antiSignals: Division is allowed and no zeros → total product ÷ nums[i] is simpler
Need contiguous-subarray products → Maximum Product Subarray (DP), not prefix/suffix
Need sums not products of all-but-self → same prefix/suffix idea but additive
remember.takeaway: Prefix/suffix accumulation answers any 'combine everything except index i' question in O(n) without division. The same two-pass scaffold underlies trapping rain water and many range-aggregate problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can avoid division and still hit O(n) by precomputing left and right partial products, and whether you can squeeze extra space to O(1) using the output array.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reaching for total-product ÷ nums[i] (fails on zeros and is explicitly forbidden), or using separate prefix and suffix arrays without collapsing them.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the two-pass solution from the definition, handle the zero cases by construction (no special-casing needed), and note the output array doesn't count as extra space.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is equal to the **product of all the elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`**.

The product of any prefix or suffix of `nums` is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer. You must write an algorithm that runs in **O(n)** time and **without using the division operation**.
constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix fits in a 32-bit integer
Follow-up: O(1) extra space (the output array does not count)
understanding: For each position, multiply together every other element. Equivalently, multiply the running product of everything to its left by the running product of everything to its right — neither of which contains the element itself.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to use division?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — it's explicitly forbidden, and it would also break when any element is zero.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain zeros?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The prefix/suffix approach handles zeros automatically: an index next to a zero still gets the correct product.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the output array count toward the space budget?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the follow-up explicitly excludes the output array, so we can store prefixes there and keep only a scalar for the suffix.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could products overflow?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The problem guarantees every prefix/suffix fits in a 32-bit int, so standard int arithmetic is safe here.

examples.explanation: Only index 2 (the position of the single zero) gets a non-zero product; every other index multiplies by that zero.
Each element's answer is just the other element.

approaches.name: Division (Why It Fails)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention only to show you know why it's banned — then discard it.
hints: The naive idea: compute the total product, then divide by each element.
What happens when an element is 0? And the problem forbids division anyway.
Use this to motivate a division-free O(n) method.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two linear passes, but it's invalid: division is disallowed and undefined for zeros.
approaches.explanation:
The tempting shortcut is `total = ∏ nums`, then `answer[i] = total / nums[i]`. It's O(n) and tiny — but it's disqualified for two reasons. First, the problem bans the division operator outright. Second, it breaks on zeros: if one element is 0 you'd divide by zero, and if two elements are 0 every answer should be 0 but the formula can't express that cleanly.

**Takeaway.** Naming this and explaining *why* it's rejected demonstrates you understood the constraints, then pivots naturally to the prefix/suffix solution.
approaches.insight: The zero cases are the real lesson: when division is unsafe, replace 'undo a global aggregate' with 'build the aggregate from the sides'. That reframing is the prefix/suffix idea.

java.line: for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) res[i] = total / nums[i]; // div by zero
java.explanation: Division is banned and crashes on any zero element — why we don't ship this.

python.line: return [total // n for n in nums]  # ZeroDivisionError on a zero
python.explanation: Forbidden operator and undefined on zeros.

pitfalls: Submitting division and getting rejected by the no-division rule.
Crashing or producing wrong output when the array contains one or more zeros.

approaches.name: Prefix × Suffix in One Array (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer — O(n) time, O(1) extra space, division-free.
hints: answer[i] = (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i). Can you precompute those?
Do a left-to-right pass writing the running prefix product into answer[i] (before multiplying in nums[i]).
Then a right-to-left pass: keep a running suffix product scalar and multiply it into answer[i] before folding nums[i] into the suffix.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two linear passes = O(n). The output array holds prefixes (doesn't count), and the suffix is a single scalar → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Define `answer[i]` as the product of all elements to the left of `i` times the product of all elements to the right. Build it in two passes:

1. **Left pass.** Maintain `prefix = 1`. For each `i` from left to right, set `answer[i] = prefix` (the product of everything strictly before `i`), then update `prefix *= nums[i]`. Crucially we write *before* multiplying, so `answer[i]` never includes `nums[i]`.
2. **Right pass.** Maintain `suffix = 1`. For each `i` from right to left, multiply `answer[i] *= suffix`, then update `suffix *= nums[i]`. Now `answer[i]` holds prefix×suffix — exactly the product of all-but-self.

**Why zeros just work.** If `nums[k] = 0`, then for any `i ≠ k` either the prefix or suffix passes through index `k` and carries the zero, making `answer[i] = 0`. Only `answer[k]` skips its own zero and survives. No special-casing needed — the structure handles it.
approaches.insight: The output array doubles as scratch space for the prefix pass, so the only extra memory is the `suffix` scalar. This 'write the partial aggregate into the result, then fold in the other direction' is the reusable shape behind many prefix/suffix problems.

dryRun.intro: Left pass fills prefixes; right pass multiplies in suffixes.

code.python:
def productExceptSelf(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    res = [1] * n
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):
        res[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        res[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return res

java.explanation: Store product of everything strictly LEFT of i (before folding nums[i] in).
Now extend the running prefix to include nums[i] for the next index.
Multiply in product of everything RIGHT of i — completes prefix×suffix.
Extend the running suffix leftward for the next index.

python.explanation: Left product for index i, excluding nums[i].
Grow prefix to include nums[i] for subsequent indices.
Fold in the right product; res[i] is now the full all-but-self product.

edgeCases.behavior: Two zeros → every answer is 0, including the zero positions (each has the other zero on one side).
Single zero → only its index gets the product of the rest (9); all others are 0.

pitfalls: Multiplying nums[i] into prefix BEFORE writing res[i] — then answer[i] wrongly includes itself.
Allocating separate prefix[] and suffix[] arrays — correct but misses the O(1)-space follow-up.
Initializing prefix/suffix to 0 instead of 1 — zeros out every product.

commonMistakes: Using division — banned by the problem and broken on zeros.
Including nums[i] in its own product by updating the running product before writing the cell.
Seeding the running products at 0 rather than 1.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Writing the cell after folding in nums[i]
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you multiply nums[i] into prefix before assigning res[i], the cell includes the element itself, which is exactly what 'except self' forbids.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
prefix *= nums[i];
res[i] = prefix; // now includes nums[i] — wrong
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
res[i] = prefix; // product of everything before i
prefix *= nums[i];

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Two extra arrays when O(1) space is asked
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Separate prefix[] and suffix[] arrays are O(n) extra space. Store prefixes in the output array and carry the suffix as a single scalar to meet the follow-up.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
prefix = [...]; suffix = [...]
res = [prefix[i] * suffix[i] for i in range(n)]
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
res = [1]*n
# left pass writes prefixes into res, right pass multiplies a scalar suffix
